summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill is part of a package that aims to cut red tape by $1 billion each year and streamline telecommunications rules while keeping consumer protections in place.

It would abolish the Telecommunications Universal Service Management Agency and move its tasks to the Department of Communications, and also transfer rules about the industry levy to the Consumer Protection Act.
The Do Not Call Register would let people sign up their phone and fax numbers forever, without needing to renew their registration.
changes: Abolishes the Telecommunications Universal Service Management Agency.
Transfers functions of the abolished agency to the Department of Communications.
Moves industry levy provisions to the Consumer Protection Act.
Makes the Do Not Call Register registration period permanent.
Relaxes pre-selection obligations on telecommunications providers.
Removes arrangements for registering e-marketing industry codes.
summary.affected: Telecommunications industry, consumers, and the Department of Communications.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation) Bill 2014, which abolishes the Telecommunications Universal Service Management Agency and transfers its functions to the department, introduces indefinite registration for the 9.3 million numbers on the Do Not Call Register saving $3.4 million a year, and delivers total expected savings of $6.9 million a year.

speeches.speaker: Jason Clare
speeches.brief: Described two minor Telecommunications deregulation bills saving about $18 million a year, listed changes including abolishing TUSMA and making Do Not Call Register listings indefinite, and said Labor would not oppose the bill after Minister Turnbull agreed to remove a schedule dealing with mandatory data retention pending a separate bill.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Criticized the government for scrapping Labor's National Broadband Network rollout plan for the Bendigo electorate without providing a replacement, describing towns including Heathcote, Kyneton, Castlemaine and Maldon dropped from the rollout map, and read a letter from the iLoddon Mallee advocacy group seeking a meeting with the Minister for Communications about the delay.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment Bill, noting the Do Not Call Register's permanent listing change follows registration by 7.3 million individuals covering 95 per cent of households, and said reduced red tape would lower industry and consumer costs by $6.9 million a year while cutting the telecommunications industry levy by $1 million.

speeches.speaker: Cathy McGowan
speeches.brief: Addressed the bill's changes to the universal service obligation, criticized Telstra's virtual monopoly on telecommunications in regional Australia, and described mobile network failures during a festival in the King Valley, noting her electorate of Indi has 275 reported mobile black spots against a national total of more than 6,000, and called for expanding the $100 million Black Spot Program.

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: Illustrated Australia's productivity problem using the abandoned Browse liquefied natural gas project at James Price Point in Western Australia, noting its onshore construction cost estimate rose from about $52 billion to about $80 billion before the joint venture partners chose a floating LNG facility instead, and noted the telecommunications bill's own savings of $6.7 million over 10 years contribute to the same productivity effort.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Henderson
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment Bill as part of the government's $2.1 billion in red tape savings, noted the Do Not Call Register's 9.3 million registrations and an extension expected to save $3.4 million a year, and cited a Geelong hire company, Kerr's Hire, that no longer must register leases under 90 days, only those over one year.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Closed debate on the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment Bill, announced the government would remove schedule 5's record-keeping requirements after industry concerns about reduced transparency and privacy, and said the remaining measures would lower industry and consumer costs by an estimated $6.71 million a year, including $3.4 million from making Do Not Call Register listings indefinite.
